title: The geography & economy of Punjab's long drug crisis
syllabus: GS3 › Linkages of organised crime with terrorism; Security challenges in border areas; Role of external state and non-state actors · GS2 › Issues relating to health; Government policies and interventions · GS1 › Social issues: youth, women · GS4 › Probity in governance
summary: An anti-drug activist's killing and a recent overdose death have put Punjab's 15-year drug crisis back at the centre of politics ahead of next year's Assembly elections.
ideas: Geography makes Punjab vulnerable: its 553-km border with Pakistan lies on the route from the Golden Crescent (Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran). Police officers call Pakistan's pushing of drugs into Punjab after militancy faded 'narco-terrorism'.
GS3 · Border security / narco-terrorism
Punjab's 553-km border with Pakistan places it on the Golden Crescent route, turning drug trafficking into a security threat.

Supply from all directions: heroin (chitta) comes across the border, opium and poppy husk from Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh (where cultivation is legal for medical use), charas from Himachal Pradesh, and pharmaceutical drugs from manufacturing hubs in neighbouring states.
GS3 · Organised crime · GS2 · Centre-state coordination
Drugs reach Punjab from across the border and from neighbouring states, so the fight needs coordination among states, not only border policing.

The problem shifts when pressed: as border enforcement improved, abuse of pharmaceutical drugs rose sharply, and smugglers turned to drones, mostly small Chinese quadcopters dropping heroin and arms, often in daylight.
GS3 · Technology and security
Each crackdown has shifted the trade to a new route, from heroin to pharma drugs and from land to drones.

Social and economic roots: opium had social acceptance even before Independence; a single run as a drug mule can earn about a lakh where jobs lag aspirations; easy, underhand wealth is increasingly accepted; whole families, including women, are drawn in.
GS1 · Youth / women · GS3 · Unemployment
Unemployment and social acceptance of easy money feed both addiction and the trade, making it a social as much as a security problem.

Enforcement first, prevention later: governments have followed the EDP model (Enforcement, De-addiction, Prevention), from a 'war on drugs' (2014) and supply crackdowns (2022) to Yudh Nasheyan Virudh (2025), which targeted drug money and moved to community action with 1.5 lakh village volunteers. Drugs remain available; observers say prevention and rehabilitation should come first.
GS2 · Government interventions / health
Enforcement alone has not ended Punjab's drug crisis; prevention and rehabilitation must lead, with enforcement in support.
keywords: Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran: one of the world's three major heroin-processing hubs
Punjab's western border sits on the Golden Crescent route, making it India's frontline against heroin.
Myanmar, Thailand and Laos: the other major heroin-producing region near India
India lies between the Golden Crescent in the west and the Golden Triangle in the east.
Using drugs to weaken a state or fund terror
Drug trafficking across Punjab's border is a form of narco-terrorism, not just crime.
Pressing one supply route pushes the trade to another
The shift from border heroin to pharma drugs shows the balloon effect of supply-only enforcement.
Medicines leaking from legal supply into addiction
Diversion of pharmaceutical drugs calls for tighter regulation of manufacturers and chemists.
Policing the trade versus reducing the need for drugs
A lasting answer must balance supply-side policing with demand-side prevention and rehabilitation.
Following the money hurts trafficking networks more than arresting carriers.
Involving local people in enforcement and prevention
Village volunteers make the anti-drug effort a community movement, not just a police drive.
data: Cases of drug possession for trafficking in Punjab in 2024, the highest in India (Uttar Pradesh next with 3,219)
Punjab recorded 6,060 drug-trafficking possession cases in 2024, the highest in India (NCRB).
Share of India's pharmaceutical drug seizures / heroin seizures in Punjab alone, 2024
Punjab alone accounted for about 57% of India's pharma drug seizures and 44% of heroin seizures in 2024.
Drone drops recorded by the BSF, 2021 to 2025
Drone drops on the Punjab border rose from 3 in 2021 to over 200 in 2025 (BSF).
Rise in arrests of women under the NDPS Act, 2015 to 2022
Arrests of women under the NDPS Act in Punjab rose 85% between 2015 and 2022.
Extension of BSF jurisdiction inland in Punjab, 2021
In 2021 the Centre extended the BSF's jurisdiction from 15 km to 50 km inland.
examples: Drone belt: Amritsar–Tarn Taran–Ferozepur–Gurdaspur
The BSF set up an anti-drone intelligence wing and Punjab Police bought anti-drone guns, yet smugglers still evade them
GS3 · Technology and security
Despite anti-drone units, drones still ferry drugs and arms across the Punjab border.
The 2013 Bhola case
A Punjab Police DSP arrested in a multimillion-rupee drug racket, convicted in 2019
GS4
GS3 · Crime nexus · GS4 · Probity
The Bhola case exposes the nexus of traffickers, police and politicians that sustains the drug trade.
Women as carriers
Traffickers use women because they are less likely to be searched; some women addicts turn peddlers
GS1 · Women / organised crime
Traffickers exploit women as carriers, adding a gender dimension to the drug trade.
1.5 lakh village volunteers
Community-driven phase of Punjab's anti-drug campaign
GS2 · People's participation
Punjab's 1.5 lakh village volunteers show community participation as part of the fight against drugs.
pyqs: The Golden Crescent next door and the links between drugs, arms and money: the Punjab border is the live case.
Drones ferrying arms and drugs: drone drops rose from 3 (2021) to over 200 (2025).
Narco-terrorism: Pakistan pushing drugs into Punjab after militancy faded.

trend.t: UPSC moved from the links between drug trafficking and other crimes (2018) to the technology that carries drugs, drones (2023), and then to narco-terrorism as a national threat (2024). GS4 also set a case study on a frontier district overrun by narcotics (2019).
trend.watch: Drugs and security have come in GS3 in 2018, 2023 and 2024, and in a GS4 case study in 2019. Narco-terrorism is a must-study area.
focus: Narco-terrorism and the Golden Crescent and Golden Triangle
Drones and technology in border smuggling
Supply-side vs demand-side strategy; de-addiction and rehabilitation

potential: Punjab's drug crisis is as much a socio-economic problem as a security challenge. Critically examine, and suggest a balanced strategy combining enforcement, de-addiction and prevention. (15 marks)
Tighter border enforcement has shifted the drug trade to pharmaceutical drugs and drones. Discuss the challenges this poses and the measures needed. (10 marks)
India lies between the Golden Crescent and the Golden Triangle. Examine the implications for its internal security. (10 marks)

practice.q: Tighter border enforcement has shifted the drug trade to pharmaceutical drugs and drones. Discuss the challenges this poses and the measures needed.
parts: Introduction: the shift in one line, with facts

answer.t: Punjab accounted for about 57% of India's pharma drug seizures in 2024, and BSF-recorded drone drops rose from 3 in 2021 to over 200 in 2025.

pts.t: Pressure on one route pushes the trade to another, so supply-only enforcement keeps chasing the problem.
pts.ex: Heroin to pharma drugs after border tightening.

pts.t: Pharma drugs come from licensed manufacturers and chemists, making them harder to police than contraband.
pts.ex: About 80% enter Punjab from hubs in neighbouring states.

pts.t: Supply comes from several states, but policing is state-wise, leaving coordination gaps.
Small quadcopters drop drugs and arms, often in daylight, and evade detection.
The same drones carry arms, tying drug smuggling to terrorism.
Collusion between traffickers, police and politicians weakens enforcement.
Track sales of habit-forming medicines from manufacturer to chemist.
Layered detection and jamming along the border, with BSF–state police coordination.
Financial investigation to break trafficking networks.
De-addiction, rehabilitation and jobs for youth, with community participation.

answer.t: Only a strategy that cuts both supply and demand can break a trade that adapts faster than enforcement.

title: Figures of gender bias, harassment are concerning: FIDE women's panel chair
syllabus: GS1 › Role of women and women's organisations; Social empowerment · GS2 › Mechanisms for the protection of vulnerable sections · GS4 › Ethics of care; Organisational accountability
summary: FIDE's first survey of women in chess found 76% faced discrimination or harassment; its women's commission chair says reporting systems must be clear, confidential and trusted.
evolution: FIDE releases its first survey on women in chess: 672 respondents from 127 federations, India the largest contributor (69).
Filed as essay data: 76% reported discrimination or harassment; 44% considered quitting; 54% never had a female mentor.
FIDE women's commission chair Tris-Ann Richards on what the figures mean and what must change.
ideas: Listen to women, not assumptions: the survey asked women directly about their experiences in the sport.
GS1 · Women's issues (method)
FIDE's first women-in-chess survey heard directly from 672 women, showing that policy must begin with women's own experiences.
The problem is not just chess: gender bias and harassment in chess mirror those in other sports, workplaces and society.
GS1 · Gender bias / patriarchy
FIDE's finding that 76% of women in chess faced discrimination or harassment mirrors bias across sport, work and society.
Reporting systems exist but do not work equally well; they must be clear, accessible, confidential and trusted.
GS2 · Protection mechanisms
Complaint systems against harassment work only when they are clear, accessible, confidential and trusted.
The real figures may be higher: women who left chess and under-18s without guardian consent are missing from the survey.
GS1 · Data gaps
Surveys of active players miss those who have already quit, so harassment may be under-counted.
Institutional ethics of care: by surveying its own players and admitting the problem, FIDE took responsibility for their safety rather than hiding it.
GS4 · Ethics of care / organisational ethics
FIDE's survey shows institutional care: an organisation listening to its members and owning the problem instead of hiding it.
keywords: 63% of women in chess reported gender bias in chess settings (FIDE, 2026).
Policies that protect athletes from abuse
Sports bodies need safeguarding systems that women trust.
Complaint channels that protect the complainant
Confidential, trusted reporting is the first step against harassment.
38% of women in chess reported online abuse or harassment.
Policy built on data from those affected
FIDE's survey shows evidence-based policy begins by listening to those affected.
data: Women in chess reporting at least one form of discrimination or harassment
76% of women in chess reported discrimination or harassment (FIDE survey, 2026).
Gender bias in chess settings / sexual harassment or inappropriate behaviour / online abuse
63% reported gender bias, 38% sexual harassment and 38% online abuse (FIDE, 2026).
examples: FIDE Women in Chess Survey (2026)
First global survey of 672 women from 127 federations; India the largest contributor
Global evidence on women in sport
FIDE's 2026 survey, with India the largest contributor, gives global evidence of bias against women in sport.
FIDE surveys and owns the problem
An institution measuring harassment in its own sport and committing to fix reporting
GS4
Institutional ethics of care
By surveying women players and admitting the figures, FIDE practised institutional accountability and care.
pyqs: Continued challenges for women 'against time and space': harassment in sport is one such space.
Gender equity needs safe spaces, not just equal entry, as the chess survey shows.
Gender justice: protection from harassment is part of the constitutional promise of dignity.
Women excel, yet social attitudes stay patriarchal: women in chess face bias despite success.

title: How these physicists brought STEM to the doorstep of women, rural youth
syllabus: GS3 › Science and technology: awareness and popularisation · GS1 › Role of women · GS2 › Education; Role of NGOs
summary: Pune-based VigyanShaala International links rural youth and young women with STEM mentors and a free AI mentor on WhatsApp; over 20,000 young women in 28 states have joined its She for STEM programme.
ideas: Mentorship closes the access gap: curious students in remote areas often lack teachers who can answer them; sustained mentoring bridges that gap.
GS3 · S&T popularisation
VigyanShaala shows that sustained mentorship can bring science to students whose schools cannot answer their questions.
Technology scales guidance: a free AI mentor on WhatsApp ('Curie') lets a student in a remote college ask a career question at midnight.
GS3 · AI for good / Digital education
AI tools like VigyanShaala's WhatsApp mentor 'Curie' can scale career guidance to remote students.
Women in STEM and first-generation learners: over 70% of the 20,000 young women in She for STEM are first-generation learners.
GS1 · Women / GS2 education
Over 70% of the 20,000 young women in She for STEM are first-generation learners, proof that mentoring widens women's access to science.
Civil society complements the state: a non-profit network of 1,000 mentors fills gaps in science education and career guidance.
GS2 · Role of NGOs
Civil-society networks like VigyanShaala complement public science education with mentorship the state cannot provide alone.
keywords: Women's participation in science, technology, engineering and maths
Mentoring and role models are key to raising women in STEM.
Students whose parents did not reach higher education
Most She for STEM participants are first-generation learners.
Encouraging children's questions builds the scientific temper the Constitution asks of citizens.
Guidance from people who have walked the path
Role models make science careers imaginable for rural girls.
Using AI to widen access, not replace people
An AI mentor on WhatsApp is an example of AI for inclusion.
data: Young women who have joined She for STEM
Over 20,000 young women across 28 states have joined She for STEM; more than 70% are first-generation learners.
examples: VigyanShaala International (Pune)
1,000 STEM mentors, a free AI mentor on WhatsApp; Nikkei Asia Prize (2025), Schlumberger Foundation's Faculty for the Future Impact Prize (2026)
Best practice in science outreach
VigyanShaala, winner of the 2025 Nikkei Asia Prize, brings STEM mentors to rural youth and women.
Diksha Nagarkoti, Pithoragarh
A girl from an Indo-Nepal border district whose teachers could not answer her questions found mentors through VigyanShaala
Human story / essay
Diksha from Pithoragarh, whose questions outran her teachers, found her path through STEM mentoring.
pyqs: Digital initiatives in education: an AI mentor on WhatsApp is one.
Education as strategic investment: building scientific talent among rural youth and women.
Gender equity in practice: targeted mentoring for young women in science.
Women's challenges 'against time and space': access to science careers in remote areas.

title: Govt to study hurdles faced by women-led informal businesses
syllabus: GS1 › Role of women; Women's issues · GS3 › Employment; Inclusive growth
context: The Statistics Ministry plans to add questions to its Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE) on 'women-specific constraints' such as restrictions on time and mobility and household responsibilities.
ideas: What is not measured is rarely fixed; better data is the first step to targeted support for women entrepreneurs.
GS1 women · GS3 inclusive growth
What is not measured is rarely fixed; MoSPI's new survey questions are a first step to supporting women entrepreneurs.
Household and care responsibilities hold back women's work; the gap is widest among the young.
GS3 · Female LFPR
Household and care duties hold back women's work most among the young.
keywords: Too little free time because of unpaid work
Time poverty from unpaid care work keeps India's women out of paid work.
Household and care work that is not paid or counted
Unpaid care work remains invisible in GDP but sustains the economy.
Gender-disaggregated data is the basis of gender-responsive policy.
Share of women working or looking for work
India's female LFPR, at 34.6% against 77.4% for men (PLFS), shows the gender gap in work.
data: Female vs male labour force participation (Sept)
Women's labour force participation is 34.6% against 77.4% for men (PLFS, September).
Among 15–29-year-olds, women's participation is just 21.5% against 61.1% for men.
About 27% of India's informal enterprises are headed by women (ASUSE 2025).
examples: MoSPI's gender-responsive survey
Adding women-specific questions to a national survey
Good governance
MoSPI's adding women-specific constraints to its enterprise survey shows the state measuring before it fixes.
pyqs: Measuring household responsibilities makes the care burden on women entrepreneurs visible.
Use the LFPR gap (34.6% women vs 77.4% men) to show equity needs targeted support.
27% of informal enterprises are headed by women; informality shapes their constraints.
summary: The Statistics Ministry will add questions on women-specific constraints (time, mobility, household duties) to its survey of informal businesses.
evolution: First Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE).
